variants.as_reported: three-base-pair deletion which results in the loss of one of a pair of highly conserved cysteine residues in the predicted third transmembrane domain of peripherin

records.segregation: Deletion segregates with the disease phenotype; absent in unaffected controls
quotes: A third adRP gene in a large Irish pedigree has been mapped to chromosome 6p, showing tight linkage with the gene for peripherin, a photoreceptor cell-specific glycoprotein, which is thus a strong candidate for the defective gene.
We have now identified a three-base-pair deletion which results in the loss of one of a pair of highly conserved cysteine residues in the predicted third transmembrane domain of peripherin.
This deletion segregates with the disease phenotype but is not present in unaffected controls, and suggests that mutant peripherin gives rise to retinitis pigmentosa.

records.label: 32 French adRP families with PRPH2 mutations
quotes: We identified 15 mutations, including 6 novel and 9 previously reported changes in 32 families, accounting for a prevalence of 10.3% in this adRP population.

Some patients characteristically showed vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. In some families, pericentral RP or macular dystrophy were found in family members while widespread RP was present in other members of the same families.

notes.statement: Manes et al. (2015) screened PRPH2 in 310 French families with autosomal dominant RP and identified 15 mutations (6 novel) in 32 families, a prevalence of 10.3%, making PRPH2 the second most frequent adRP gene after RHO in their series.
quotes: PRPH2 was screened by Sanger sequencing in a cohort of 310 French families with adRP.

The mutations in PRPH2 account for 10.3% of adRP in the French population, which is higher than previously reported (0%-8%) This makes PRPH2 the second most frequent adRP gene after RHO in our series.

notes.statement: Manes et al. (2015) showed that a recurrent novel PRPH2 mutation, leu254-to-gln (L254Q), expressed in yeast led to protein aggregation, suggesting abnormal folding.
quotes: We showed that a new recurrent p.Leu254Gln mutation leads to protein aggregation, suggesting abnormal folding.
Peripherin-2 protein was produced in yeast and analyzed by Western blot.

notes.statement: Manes et al. (2015) found that PRPH2-associated adRP was of moderate severity, with 78% of eyes having visual acuity of 1-0.5 and 52% retaining more than 50% of the visual field; phenotypes were highly variable, with pericentral RP or macular dystrophy and widespread RP occurring within the same families. They suggested that mild cases could be underdiagnosed.
quotes: The clinical severity of the disease in examined patients was moderate with 78% of the eyes having 1-0.5 of visual acuity and 52% of the eyes retaining more than 50% of the visual field.
PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes and moderate forms of adRP, including mild cases, which could be underdiagnosed.

notes.statement: Wang et al. (2013) identified homozygous PRPH2 missense mutations in 3 patients with LCA or juvenile RP: p.C213R in 1 patient and p.L185P, previously reported in digenic RP with a ROM1 null mutation, in 2 patients. The authors concluded that homozygous mutations in PRPH2 cause early-onset retinal dystrophy with LCA/juvenile RP phenotypes.
quotes: The p.C213R mutation is associated with autosomal dominant pattern dystrophy, and the p.L185P mutation, together with a null mutation in ROM1, has been reported to cause digenic RP.
To our knowledge, our study reported for the first time that homozygous mutations in PRPH2 cause EORD with LCA/juvenile RP phenotypes.

notes.statement: Wang et al. (2013) found that heterozygous carriers of PRPH2 mutations in the families of the homozygous patients had no symptoms but showed macular pattern dystrophy, for example the 56-year-old father of a p.L185P homozygote. The authors suggested a dose-dependent effect and proposed that heterozygous p.L185P carriers in digenic RP families may have a subclinical phenotype.
quotes: For example, the 56-year-old father of patient 741 had macular pattern dystrophy and clear-cut foveal changes, but his visual acuity was essentially normal in both eyes
Taken together, these findings suggest that, although asymptomatic, individuals harbouring the heterozygous p.L185P mutation should be expected to exhibit a subclinical phenotype

notes.statement: Wells et al. (1993) found that RDS mutations caused either retinitis pigmentosa or macular dystrophy. Three families with similar macular dystrophy had mutations at codon 172: arg172 to trp in two families and arg172 to gln in one. A stop codon at codon 258 was found in a family with adult vitelliform macular dystrophy. The authors suggested that certain amino acids in peripherin-RDS may have different functional significance in cones and rods.
quotes: Three families with similar macular dystrophy have mutations at codon 172, arginine being substituted by tryptophan in two and by glutamine in one.
A stop sequence at codon 258 exists in a family with adult vitelliform macular dystrophy.
the functional significance of certain amino-acids in peripherin-RDS may be different in cones and rods

notes.statement: Weleber et al. (1993) concluded that a 3-bp deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the peripherin/RDS gene can produce clinically disparate phenotypes even within one family. In the family they studied, these phenotypes were retinitis pigmentosa, pattern macular dystrophy and fundus flavimaculatus.
quotes: A 3-base pair deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the peripherin/RDS gene can produce clinically disparate phenotypes even within the same family.
We report herein the occurrence of three separate phenotypes within a single family with a novel 3-base pair deletion of codon 153 or 154 of the peripherin/RDS gene.

notes.statement: Kajiwara et al. (1994) found 3 families in which retinitis pigmentosa developed only in individuals who were double heterozygotes for mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, establishing digenic inheritance of RP.
quotes: Three families were identified with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, in which only double heterozygotes develop retinitis pigmentosa (RP).

notes.statement: Kajiwara et al. (1994) concluded that the allelic and nonallelic heterogeneity of monogenic RP is further complicated by interactions between unlinked mutations causing digenic RP.
quotes: These findings indicate that the allelic and nonallelic heterogeneity known to be a feature of monogenic RP is complicated further by interactions between unlinked mutations causing digenic RP.

notes.statement: Kikawa et al. (1994) found the Asn244Lys mutation in the peripherin/RDS gene using nonradioactive single-strand conformation polymorphism (SSCP) analysis.
quotes: A novel mutation (Asn244Lys) in the peripherin/RDS gene causing autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa associated with bull's-eye maculopathy detected by nonradioisotopic SSCP.

notes.statement: Farrar et al. (1991) mapped an autosomal dominant RP locus to chromosome 6p in an Irish family with late-onset ADRP. Two-point lod scores were positive with several markers, including D6S105 (Z = 6.081 at theta = 0.00) and RDS (Z = 5.376 at theta = 0.00). Multipoint analysis gave a maximum lod score of 6.6 at HLA-DRA.
quotes: Positive two-point lod scores have been obtained with five markers (D6S89: theta = 0.10, Z = 3.338; D6S109: theta = 0.10, Z = 3.932; D6S105: theta = 0.00, Z = 6.081; HLA-DRA: theta = 0.00, Z = 4.364; and RDS: theta = 0.00, Z = 5.376).
In a series of overlapping multipoint analyses a lod score of 6.6 was obtained, maximizing at HLA-DRA and hence localizing the ADRP gene (RP5) segregating in this pedigree to 6p.

notes.statement: Farrar et al. (1991) concluded that their data provided direct evidence for an additional autosomal dominant RP locus. They stated that the data strongly implicated peripherin-rds, the human equivalent of the mouse retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene, as a candidate gene.
quotes: These data provide direct evidence for an additional autosomal dominant RP locus and strongly implicate the human equivalent of the mouse retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene, peripherin-rds, as a candidate for autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa.

notes.statement: Farrar et al. (1991) reported that a third adRP gene in a large Irish pedigree mapped to chromosome 6p and was tightly linked to the gene for peripherin, a photoreceptor cell-specific glycoprotein. This made peripherin a strong candidate gene.
quotes: A third adRP gene in a large Irish pedigree has been mapped to chromosome 6p, showing tight linkage with the gene for peripherin, a photoreceptor cell-specific glycoprotein, which is thus a strong candidate for the defective gene.

notes.statement: Farrar et al. (1991) noted that autosomal dominant RP is genetically heterogeneous. Loci had been mapped to chromosome 3q near the rhodopsin gene, to chromosome 8p, and to chromosome 6p.
quotes: We mapped the first autosomal dominant RP (adRP) gene to chromosome 3q, close to the gene encoding rhodopsin, a rod photoreceptor pigment protein.
Another adRP gene has been mapped to chromosome 8p.

notes.statement: Kajiwara et al. (1991) found 3 mutations in the human homolog of the mouse rds gene (RDS), each cosegregating with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in a separate family. They concluded that some cases of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa are due to mutations at the RDS locus.
quotes: We report here three mutations of the human homologue of the rds gene (RDS) that cosegregate with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in separate families.
Our results indicate that some cases of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa are due to mutations at the RDS locus.

notes.statement: Kajiwara et al. (1991) noted that the mouse retinal degeneration slow (rds) mutation is semidominant. In rds mice, rod and cone photoreceptors develop abnormally and then slowly degenerate, which made the mouse a possible model for retinitis pigmentosa.
quotes: The murine retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene is a semidominant mutation with a phenotype having rod and cone photoreceptors that develop abnormally and then slowly degenerate. The phenotype is a possible model for retinitis pigmentosa

notes.statement: In a large Irish family with late-onset autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa linked to 6p, Jordan et al. (1992) found that an intragenic marker from the peripherin-RDS gene cosegregated with the disease with zero recombination (lod score 5.46 at theta = 0.00). They mapped the peripherin-RDS gene against other 6p markers using the CEPH reference panel. In multipoint analysis, the lod score reached 8.21 and peaked at the peripherin-RDS locus.
quotes: an intrageneic marker derived from this gene cosegregated with the adRP disease locus with zero recombination (lod score 5.46 at q = .00)
Incorporation of these data into a multipoint analysis produced a lod score for adRP of 8.21, maximizing at the peripherin-RDS locus.

notes.statement: Jordan et al. (1992) concluded that their results gave strong evidence for a role of peripherin-RDS, a photoreceptor-specific protein, in the cause of one form of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa.
quotes: This study provides strong evidence suggesting a role for peripherin-RDS in the etiology of one form of adRP.
